strengths: The paper targets a useful computer-vision problem: combining map imagery, camera observations, and geospatial signals for conversational place understanding and pedestrian assistance.

IMAIA is a coherent end-to-end prototype. Its grid-based map grounding, image/place reranking, multi-agent orchestration, and distilled spatial module address complementary parts of the user workflow.

Maps Plus reports a large improvement over its GPT-4o baselines on 4,300 queries (89.83% versus 39.30–42.74%), suggesting that explicit entity retrieval can substantially improve view-conditioned map QA.

The spatial distillation pipeline is practically motivated and reasonably concrete: it uses 40,000 street-view images, entity mining, open-vocabulary localization, depth estimation, relational annotation, and Florence-2 fine-tuning. The reported 1.7-second inference time is promising for interactive use.
The manuscript communicates the system architecture clearly through diagrams and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central claims are not supported by sufficiently rigorous evaluation. The Maps Plus benchmark consists of synthetic queries generated from POI attributes using GPT-4o, but the paper does not describe train/test separation, query validation, answer scoring, sampling per city, map scale, repeated-run variance, or safeguards against the queried geospatial service directly returning the target used to construct each question. Only weak variants of the same GPT-4o setup are compared, with no established map-grounding or geospatial QA baseline.

Table II appears internally inconsistent. Each query is described as having one manually annotated ground-truth venue, in which case Precision@1 must equal Recall@1 and Recall@3 should equal three times Precision@3 under the paper's definitions. The reported pairs, such as 80.4%/72.5% at top-1 and 36.2%/92.8% at top-3, cannot follow those definitions. This calls the venue-ranking results into question.

The navigation evidence is anecdotal. Claims that the method reduces detours, aligns better with pedestrian behavior, and improves usability are based on a single illustrated route; there is no user study, route-length measurement, success rate, sensor-error analysis, comparison across environments, or safety evaluation. Direction-only guidance may encourage traversal through non-walkable or unsafe areas.

The spatial-understanding evaluation is under-specified and potentially biased. Accuracy is assigned by a proprietary o1 LLM judge without its rubric, prompt, repeated judgments, or human agreement. The provenance and separation of the 400-image test set from the 40,000 training images are not stated. An average of seven predicted objects versus four from ASM v2 is not evidence of higher recall without annotated ground-truth objects, and the 84% versus 27% comparison covers only one general VLM.

The latency comparison is not controlled: a local distilled model is compared with an agent pipeline making unspecified external model calls, so the 7.3× speedup conflates architecture, model, hardware, and service latency. No memory, throughput, cost, or variability measurements are supplied.

The technical description is insufficient for reproduction. Missing details include prompts, grid resolution and viewport processing, Azure candidate-retrieval parameters, exact CLIP variant, candidate-set construction, circular treatment of heading differences, XGBoost configuration, Florence-2 training hyperparameters, dataset splits, judge protocol, and code/data availability.

The originality is primarily systems integration of existing APIs, pretrained encoders, XGBoost, multi-agent routing, and knowledge distillation. That integration could be useful, but the manuscript does not isolate which components cause the gains through ablations or establish a clear methodological advance over existing grounded map and spatial-reasoning systems.

Presentation issues—including grammatical errors, malformed citations such as the YOLO-World reference, and imprecise terminology—are correctable, but the decisive concern is the validity and completeness of the empirical evidence rather than writing quality. Overall, the prototype has merit, yet the inconsistent retrieval metrics and inadequate validation of its principal claims make the current balance favor rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: connecting conversational map exploration, camera-based place recognition, and pedestrian guidance in one system.

The proposed system is intuitively organized into map grounding, venue ranking, navigation, and spatial-understanding components, with intermediate agent decisions that could improve interpretability.

The reported component-level results are promising in magnitude: Maps Plus reaches 89.83% accuracy versus 39.30–42.74% for its baselines, the XGBoost ranker improves top-k results, and the distilled model reports a 7.3× inference speedup.

The manuscript includes understandable system diagrams, interface examples, dataset sizes, and inference hardware information. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/2488433a0d884333b278de4bca957acf/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The main Maps Plus evaluation is potentially circular. GPT-4o generates synthetic questions from POI attributes, coordinates, and contextual data, while the proposed method retrieves related entities from a geospatial index and injects them into GPT-4o. The paper does not explain how leakage is prevented, how answers are scored, or whether queries were independently validated. The baselines lack access to the retrieval information provided to the proposed method, so the experiment primarily demonstrates the benefit of privileged external data rather than a controlled comparison with strong retrieval-augmented systems.

Table II appears internally inconsistent or insufficiently defined. Each image query is described as having one ground-truth venue, in which case Precision@1 and Recall@1 should coincide, yet the table reports 80.4% versus 72.5% for XGBoost. Moreover, a 50-query test set would normally yield top-1 rates in two-percentage-point increments, which does not explain several reported values. No averaging protocol, number of candidates, confidence intervals, or repeated splits are given.

The spatial-understanding result is not adequately substantiated. The 84% figure relies entirely on an unspecified o1 LLM-as-judge protocol: the number and type of questions, judge prompt, scoring rubric, human agreement, and relationship between the 400 test images and the 40,000-image training source are omitted. The only general-model comparison is Florence-VL 8B at 27%, while the ASM v2 comparison uses object count rather than spatial-reasoning accuracy. There is no comparison to the GPT-4o teacher or to the cited SpatialVLM and SpatialRGPT methods on a shared benchmark.

The navigation claims are unsupported by an experiment. Reduced detours, greater naturalness, and alignment with pedestrian behavior are inferred from a single illustrated route; there is no user study, route set, distance/time measurement, success rate, or safety analysis. Direction-only guidance may encourage crossing open or non-walkable areas, making the absence of safety evaluation especially consequential.

The claimed unified system is never evaluated end to end. The experiments test isolated pieces with different datasets and metrics, and there is no evidence that integrating Maps Plus and PAISA improves task completion, latency, robustness, or user experience. Likewise, there is no ablation showing that the multi-agent architecture is preferable to a simpler pipeline.

Originality is limited at the method level. Most elements combine established components—GPT-4o prompting, grid overlays, Azure Maps retrieval, CLIP features, XGBoost ranking, YOLO-World, Depth Anything, and Florence-2 distillation. The paper does not clearly isolate a novel algorithmic contribution or experimentally establish that its particular integration is technically superior to standard retrieval/tool-using alternatives.

Reproducibility is poor. The paper omits prompts, grid resolution and entity-extraction details, query-generation and annotation procedures, train/test splits, XGBoost configuration, candidate generation, Florence-2 optimization settings, judge protocol, API/version details, and cost analysis. Reliance on proprietary models, Azure search activity, and undisclosed data compounds the issue; no code or dataset release is specified.

Several technical and reporting details require correction. The bearing equation is written as an ambiguous two-argument arctangent, latitude/longitude conversion to radians is not stated, and heading consistency is defined as an absolute angular difference without specifying circular wrap-around. The manuscript also contains numerous grammatical errors and malformed text, although these presentation issues are secondary to the experimental deficiencies.

Overall, the paper presents an appealing prototype and promising preliminary numbers, but the central claims rest on uncontrolled synthetic evaluation, internally unclear metrics, incomparable baselines, and anecdotal navigation evidence. These are material validity problems rather than merely limited evaluation breadth, so the current evidence does not support acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision application by connecting map-conditioned question answering, camera-based venue grounding, spatial scene understanding, and pedestrian guidance in one interactive system.

Maps Plus reports a large improvement over the same-backbone baselines on 4,300 queries (89.83% versus 39.30–42.74%), suggesting that explicit map grids and geospatial retrieval can substantially improve view-conditioned place identification.

The location-intelligence ranker sensibly combines complementary visual and geospatial signals: CLIP similarity, distance, heading consistency, and popularity priors. Its reported ranking results improve over either distance-only or similarity-only ranking.

Distilling the spatial module into Florence-2 is practically motivated. The reported 1.7-second inference time versus 12.4 seconds for the agent pipeline is relevant to interactive deployment, and the paper communicates the overall system workflow with helpful interface examples.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is not yet reliable enough to support the main claims. The Maps Plus benchmark uses GPT-4o to synthesize questions from POI attributes and contextual information, but the paper does not describe answer construction, scoring, filtering, train/test separation, geographic diversity beyond ten US cities, or safeguards against leaking the answer through retrieved entities. Consequently, the nearly 90% accuracy is difficult to interpret.

Table II appears internally inconsistent with the stated evaluation. Each query is described as having a ground-truth venue, in which case Precision@1 and Recall@1 should coincide, yet the XGBoost values are 80.4% and 72.5%. Likewise, the Top-3 precision and recall figures do not have the relationship implied by a single relevant venue. The number of relevant venues per query and aggregation method are not explained, making this result unverifiable.

The spatial-understanding evaluation is seriously underspecified. It uses only 400 street-view images, does not establish that they are independent of the 40,000-image distillation corpus, and reports accuracy from an o1 LLM judge without prompts, repeated judging, human validation, agreement measurements, uncertainty, or a precise correctness rubric.

The spatial comparisons do not constitute a controlled benchmark: accuracy is compared mainly with Florence-VL, object count is used as a proxy for recall against ASM v2 without establishing correctness, and latency is compared with an agent pipeline performing different operations. Important references such as the GPT-4o teacher, Florence-2 without distillation, and stronger spatial VLMs are not evaluated under common metrics.

The claimed navigation advantages—reduced detours, greater flexibility, and better alignment with pedestrian behavior—are supported only by a single qualitative example. There is no route-length analysis, success rate, localization-error study, safety evaluation, or user study. Directly pointing toward a destination can also encourage passage through non-walkable or unsafe areas.

Some technical details are problematic or incomplete. The bearing equation should explicitly use atan2 rather than an ordinary arctangent, and heading differences require circular normalization; otherwise angles near 0/360 degrees are handled incorrectly. Sensor noise and magnetic-heading uncertainty are not considered.

The work is largely an integration of existing proprietary models, APIs, retrieval, ranking, and multi-agent orchestration. That integration may be useful, but the paper does not clearly isolate a novel technical contribution through component ablations. Reproducibility is also poor because code, data, prompts, annotation procedures, XGBoost settings, Florence-2 training hyperparameters, API versions, costs, and end-to-end latency are absent. These are material scientific limitations; the numerous grammatical and typesetting issues are secondary presentation concerns.
